metadata.title: Evolutionary Multi-Agent Deep Meta Reinforcement Learning Method for Swarm Intelligence Energy Management of Isolated Multi-Area Microgrid With Internet of Things
metadata.abstract_summary: This article proposes a swarm intelligence load frequency control method for isolated multi-area microgrids, which reduces communication burden and improves robustness. The method is demonstrated to be effective in a simulation of a four-area LFC model for Sansha island in the China Southern Grid.

sections.heading: Multi-Area Microgrid With Internet of Things
sections.text: Jiawen Li and Tao Zhou Abstract —In an isolated multiarea microgrid, a conventional centralized active control policy relies on excessive communica- tion and therefore is incapable of coordinating the interests of multiple operators. For this reason, this article proposes a swarm intelligence load frequency control (SI-LFC) method. Based on the swarm intelligence method, the proposed method equates the units in each area as independent agents and adopts the swarm intelligence centralized offline learning policy to achieve the balance of interests of different operators. In an online appli- cation, each unit only needs to collect the frequency locally to achieve global optimal control, thereby reducing the communica- tion burden across the network. In addition, this article proposes an evolutionary multiagent deep meta-actor–critic (EMA-DMAC) algorithm, which introduces meta-reinforcement learning and evolutionary learning to achieve fast collaborative learning of swarm agents, thereby improving the robustness and quality of the obtained SI-LFC strategies. The effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated in a simulation of the four-area LFC model for Sansha island in the China Southern Grid (CSG). Index Terms —Active control, distributed optimization, evolu- tionary multiagent deep meta actor critic (EMA-DMAC), isolated multiarea microgrid, load frequency control. I. I NTRODUCTION I N RECENT years, driven by economic factors and envi- ronmental issues, governments and research institutions have increasingly prioritized the development of renewable energy technologies for the purposes of energy restructuring and sustainable social development [ 1 ]. Since the substitution of renewable energy sources (including solar, wind, geother- mal, biomass, and other nonfossil energy sources) for fossil fuels significantly reduces carbon emissions, distributed gen- erators (DGs) technologies based on renewable energy sources have received much attention among academics and industry stakeholders. As their proportion in the conventional grid increases, they inevitably have a stronger impact upon the grid [ 2 ]. In order to identify a suitable medium in the spectrum from large con- ventional grids to DG-based grids, and to fully exploit the value and benefits of DGs to grids, the Consortium for Electric Reliability Technology Solutions proposed the concept of the microgrid [ 3 ], in which DGs are integrated effectively with traditional large grids. However, one of the key issues which remains unsolved in the actual operation of MG systems is the inadequacy of conventional control methods. The main control variables include frequency and active power [ 4 ]. In the islanding mode the large grid cannot provide support for MGs, and the DG characteristics and loads in MGs change fre- quently; altogether, these factors make the control of islanded MGs challenging [ 5 ]. A reasonable and reliable coordinated control policy for DGs is needed to maintain the stability of the frequency and voltage of the islanded MGs, and ensure reasonable distribution of active and reactive power [ 6 ]. Microgrid Model According to Fig. 1 , the isolated multiarea microgrid system is designed for microgrids containing distributed energy sources to improve the microgrid energy utilization effi- ciency by local consumption of distributed power output under the constraints of system operation. For different capacity microgrids, diesel generators, micro turbines (MT), and fuel cells (FCs) are selected as regulating units to ensure frequency stability in order to match the uncontrollable new energy gen- eration and load power. However, the random of wind turbine (WT), photovoltaic (PV), and load will lead to frequent power shortage in the system. Areas are interconnected by tie lines, and frequency changes in each individual area affect the frequency of the area with which it is interconnected. SI-LFC Framework Microgrids are decentralized and therefore require flexible control, a criterion which cannot be satisfied using centralized dispatch. Therefore, in the policy design, some control rights are delegated to certain control devices inside the microgrid, conferring on them autonomous control rights within certain management limits. This will greatly simplify the control model and thus prevent the problems attendant with centralized control of the large number of operations. Decentralized control leads to improved response speed, and, whenever a grid fluctuation occurs, the corresponding action will be issued quickly to ensure system stability. For the method proposed in this article, group intelligence is introduced into LFC to form SI-LFC, under which each unit in each area is equated as an independent agent. SI-LFC uses the centralized offline learning policy based on group intelligence to balance of interests of different operators and improve the global frequency regulation performance. In an online appli- cation, each unit in each area only needs to collect frequency locally, reducing communication pressure in the realization of global optimal control. There is no need for communication between agents, nor is there any communication between zones. The units make decisions completely autonomously and independently, a key characteristic of group intelligence. The control interval of each agent is 4 s. Each agent collects the microgrid sta- tus separately to calculate the power command for each unit. SI-LFC has the advantages of autonomy, spontaneity, and fast response of the agent units, and can decompose the complex and huge overall control of the whole grid into decen- tralized control of small units. sections.text: C ASE 1 For Area B, the EMA-DMAC algorithm has the smallest frequency deviation, while the frequency deviations for the other algorithms are 1.99–3.82 times that of EMA-DMAC. Compared to that of the other algorithms, the total unit generation cost of EMA-DMAC is 3.93%–4.21% lower. For Area C, the EMA-DMAC algorithm has the smallest frequency deviation, while the frequency deviations for the other algorithms are 1.01–2.96 times that of EMA-DMAC. Compared to that of the other algorithms, the total unit generation cost of EMA-DMAC is 0.11%–0.12% lower. For Area D, the EMA-DMAC algorithm has the smallest frequency deviation, while the frequency deviations for the other algorithms are 1.00–2.97 times that of EMA-DMAC. The total unit generation cost of EMA-DMAC is the lowest out of all the algorithms ($249.78). As mentioned, the EMA-DMAC algorithm adopts a fully distributed LFC structure, equates the units as independent decision-making agents, and uses evolutionary learning and meta-learning techniques to help multiple agents to learn and obtain a control policy with higher robustness and adap- tive capability. During multiple stochastic disturbances, the EMA-DMAC policy ensures greater performance compared to that of the other algorithms. Thus, as indicated in Fig. 8 (a) and (b), the frequency deviation of the EMA-DMAC algorithm is able to respond quickly and recover quickly, due to the correct regulation of the total regulation output by the control pol- icy. According to Fig. 8 (c), the EMA-DMAC algorithm has a faster response in terms of total regulated output and carries no output overshoot, and the units are not subject to double regu- lation, leading to the lower generation cost. The EMA-DMAC algorithm adopts a large number of fast units for outputting at the beginning of the disturbance, and a small number of fast and low-cost units for outputting at the end of the disturbance, which explain the generation cost. In addition, application of the EMA-DMAC algorithm results in lower generation cost as EMA-DMAC enables the agents of multiarea microgrids to coordinate with each other. According to Fig. 8 (d), the improvement in the frequency regulation performance across the areas leads to the reduction in tie-line power, which in turn leads to reduced fluctuation of frequency deviation across the areas. Compared to EMA-DMAC, the performance of the other DRL algorithms is generally inferior, as shown in Fig. 8 (a)–(d). Those DRL algorithms lack suitable bootstrap- ping techniques, which leads to low robustness and more limited convergence. In the face of disturbances, these algo- rithms struggle to realize effective collaboration of multiple agents, especially when there are many agents. As shown in Fig. 8 (c), this leads to overshoot of the total regulation out- put in each area, which in turn leads to frequency deviation oscillations with tie-line power fluctuations [Fig. 8 (d)]. These unfavorable factors explain their inferior global frequency regulation performance, which in turn leads to duplicate regulation of units and increased generation costs. Other centralized LFCs experience fluctuations in regula- tion commands due to conflicting objectives of controllers and distributors, which in turn lead to fluctuations in the total regu- lation output and large oscillations in frequency deviation and tie-line power. Compared to that of the other algorithms, the total unit generation cost of EMA-DMAC is 24.5%–34.3% lower. In summary, when multiple disturbances are applied to the multiarea microgrid, the EMA-DMAC algorithm carries the lowest frequency deviation and generation cost across all four areas. The EMA-DMAC algorithm uses multiple techniques to enhance the coordination of the agents, so that these multiple agents are globally optimized in offline training and can consider each other’s strategies. When applied online, each agent can make decisions independently by simply collect- ing data on local states. This results in no communication at all being required of the control, which greatly reduces com- munication pressure and circumvents the frequency error and increased generation cost attendant to the inconsistent objec- tives of the controller and distributor in a centralized LFC architecture. According to Fig. 9 (b), the overshoot and fluctuations of the total regulated output of the EMA-DMAC algorithm are significantly less than those of the other algorithms, as it is able to stabilize the total regulated output during rapid load changes. This explains the lower frequency deviation of the EMA-DMAC algorithm, which in turn is due to the dis- tributed LFC policy employed by the EMA-DMAC algorithm. EMA-DMAC is able to invoke a large number of fast units for power generation at the beginning of the disturbance and low-cost units for power generation at the end of the distur- bance, thus reducing the total generation cost and balancing the interests of grid operators in each area. The EMA-DMAC policy reduces tie-line power fluctuations, so that each area does not have to pay too much in support, thus reducing the conflict of interest. Moreover, the effective policy reduces the duplication of unit regulation, which can reduce generation costs. By comparison, the other DRL algorithms exhibited weaker robustness. During the stochastic disturbances their total mod- ulation output exhibits overshoot, which in turn leads to an increase in frequency error [Fig. 9 (a)].
